lawyer:
Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, Advocate — For the Petitioners.
Kh Mahbubuddin Ahmed, with Sahabuddin Foez, Advocates — For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Chittagong Development Authority, represented by its Chairman and others ------ Petitioner
Vs. 
Rokeya Anwar and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 15-3-90 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 109 of 1989 affirming the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in other Suit No. 96 of 1978 decreeing the suit. 

 2. Opposite Party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted a suit in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong, being Other Suit No. 96 of 1978, praying for declaration of title and mandatory injunction alleging, inter alia, that suit plot No. 489 in Agrabad Residential Area, Chittagong was settled with Mofazal Ahmed and Fazal Hoque, defendant Nos. 7 and 8 respectively and they owned and possessed the same. Subsequently on taking permission from the Chittagong Development Authority (CDA) defendant Nos. 7 and 8 transferred the suit land to plaintiff No. 1 and in the lease deed in question 4.666 kathas of land was mentioned. In course of time the plaintiff constructed pucca buildings in the said premises and since then she has been residing therein. It has been further contended that at the time of construction of the house it was detected that the suit land actually comprises more than 4.666 kathas as mentioned in the deed of lease, following which the plaintiff filed an application before the CDA for granting her lease of the excess land in terms of the conditions embodied in the deed of agreement but the CDA instead of allowing the said prayer for lease of the excess land directed the plaintiff by letter dated 27-11-88 to surrender the excess land to the CDA and this necessitated the filing of the suit. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 1-5 contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that suit plot No. 489 with an area of 4.696 kathas only was leased out to the vendors of the plaintiff and the area of the land settled was specifically mentioned in the lease deed as 4.696 kathas of land and, as such, the plaintiff''s claim for more than 4.696 kathas of land cannot be entertained. It was further contended that the quantum of land allotted to the settle was clearly and specifically mentioned in the lease deed in terms of the lease agreement and the site-map and the sketch-map appended thereto are mere indications for the purpose of identification of the land settled and these by no means indicate the actual quantum of land demised. It was further contended that the plaintiff illegally encroached upon the land of schedule No. 2 to the plaint, in which she has no title and interest. Since the suit land as described in Schedule No. 2 to the plaint is admittedly the land of the Chittagong Development Authority, which fact has not been denied by the plaintiff or her predecessors-in-interest, the plaintiff cannot claim this excess land as a matter of right and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 1) Is the suit maintainable in its present form? 

 2) Has the plaintiff any cause of action to file the present suit? 

 3) Whether the plaintiff has any title, interest and possession in the suit property? and 

 4) To what relief, if any, the plaintiff is entitled to? 

 5. At the trial the plaintiff examined two witnesses and the contesting defendant examined four witnesses and exhibited documents in support of their respective cases. The learned Assistant Judge by the impugned judgment dated 31-1-89 decreed the suit and directed defendant Nos. 1-5 for giving settlement of the land of Schedule 2 to the plaint to the plaintiff within 60 days of the decree. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendant petitioners took an appeal before the District Judge, Chittagong, who was pleased by the impugned judgment dated 15-3-93 to dismiss the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. It is to be noted in this connection that the trial Court while decreeing the suit did not declare the plaintiff''s title in the suit land, which tantamount to rejection of the plaintiff's prayer for declaration of her title in the suit land. It appears from the record that the plaintiff did not prefer any cross-objection against it after defendant-petitioners preferred Other Class Appeal No. 109 of 1989 before the District Judge, Chittagong and, as such, the plaintiff is deemed to have accepted the said refusal to declare her title in the suit land gracefully. 

 7. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioners, submits that the learned Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit without noticing and considering that the suit was clearly barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that the learned Courts below seriously erred in law in holding that the boundaries of the suit land shall prevail over the area of the land mentioned in the lease agreement Ext. 2 and Ext. A, which clearly show that only 4.96 kathas of land in suit plot No. 489 was settled with the allotees, who are the vendors of the present plaintiff, and possession of the said land was made over to them and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr Bhuiyan further submits that in the face of the admitted fact that 4.966 kathas of land in suit plot No. 489 was settled with the plaintiff by lease agreement Ext. 2, and the plaintiff prayed for settlement of lease of the excess amount of land measuring 4.80 square feet and for a declaration of title over the excess amount of land than originally settled, the suit for declaration of title and permanent injunction relating to the said excess land is not contemplated in law and, as such, the learned Courts below misdirected themselves to decree the suit on an erroneous view of law and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr Bhuiyan further submits that the lay-out plan, site-map, etc. merely indicate the location and identification of the suit land and not the quantum of land settled with the allottees, which was specifically mentioned in the lease deed as 4.966 kathas of land only, and the plaintiff accepted the same and acted upon the same taking it to be so, as has been specifically admitted in paragraph 9 of the plaint, and consequently, the plaintiffs claim of title in the excess land is not contemplated in law and the learned Courts below clearly erred in law in decreeing the suit completely ignoring the scope of the suit and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that in view of the admitted fact that no vested right was created in favour of the plaintiff for getting settlement of Schedule 2 land and there was no corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the said land in favour of the plaintiff, the learned Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit completely ignoring this material aspect of the case and the law bearing on the subject and the same has occasioned failure of justice. 

 8. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party, on the other hand, submits that the learned Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff is entitled to get settlement of Schedule 2 land and the impugned judgment thus being concluded by concurrent findings of fact is not to be interfered with by this Court exercising power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Khondker further submits that although the trial Court and, as a matter of fact, the appellate Court did not declare the plaintiff's title in the suit land, nevertheless there was a prayer for declaration of plaintiff''s title in the suit land and, as such, in the facts and circumstance of the case and the evidence on record, the plaintiff''s title in the suit land can be declared by this Court exercising revisional power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Khondker further submits that since the plaintiff was successful in proving her case the suit has rightly been decreed and the said decree cannot be interfered with in revision as it has not occasioned any failure of justice. 

 9. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, has taken me through the impugned judgment. I also heard the learned Advocates of the contending parties extensively. In the impugned judgment of the trial Court the learned Assistant Judge found, as has been specifically mentioned in paragraph No. 9 of the plaint, that the plaintiff took settlement of 4.966 kathas of land and she acted on the same premises without any reservation but at the time of physical measurement it transpired that the suit land actually measured 5.666 kathas and not 4.966 kathas of land as mentioned in the lease deed Ext. 2 and for the excess land measuring 4.80 sqft she promptly prayed for settlement from the CDA on usual terms and conditions but on refusal of the defendants to settle the excess land to the plaintiff, she was constrained to file the present suit. 

 10. It appears that the learned trial Court without discussing and considering the oral evidence of the two PWs and four DWs and without considering the exhibited documents decreed the suit directing the defendants to settle the excess land measuring 4.80 sqft to the plaintiff on usual terms and conditions without spelling out anything as to how the plaintiff acquired a vested right in the said land and the CDA was under a legal obligation to grant lease of the said land to the plaintiff. 

 11. While disposing of the appeal the learned Additional District Judge also failed to discuss and consider any evidence of the 6 witnesses examined by the contending parties and dismissed the appeal on the finding that the plaintiff being in possession of Schedule 2 land as an integral part of Schedule 1 land has become the rightful owner of the scheduled land and, as such, she was entitled to get lease of Schedule 2 land on payment of proportionate premium to the CDA. The learned Additional District Judge further held that the boundary of the suit land will prevail over the area mentioned in the lease deed Ext. 2. From the impugned judgments it appears that neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court took the pains of discussing and considering the material evidence of the 6 witnesses examined by the contending parties. 

 13. The moot question in this case is as to whether the plaintiff has any vested legal right in claiming the settlement of Schedule 2 land and whether the defendant CDA was under any legal obligation to grant lease of the excess land contained in Schedule 2 of the plaint in favour of the plaintiff. In the absence of any vested legal right on the part of the plaintiff and a corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the excess land in favour of the plaintiff, the plaintiff's claim for settlement cannot be entertained. Neither the trial Court nor the lower appellate Court appeal's to have addressed itself to this vital question nor has it drawn any conclusion on it on the basis of the evidence on record. Nowhere in the impugned judgments it is found that the learned Courts below held that the plaintiff is entitled to get settlement of the suit land as of right and the CDA is under a legal obligation to make such settlement. The plaintiff did not make out any case of adverse possession, establishing any claim for life. 

 14. In paragraph No. 9 of the plaint it has been specifically mentioned that the plaintiff bona fide believed that she took the settlement of only 4.999 kathas of land from the CDA and acting on the said premises she owned and possessed the suit land but while taking actual measurement of the suit land at the time of construction of her house it was detected that the suit land actually measured 5.666 kathas and not 4.966 kathas as mentioned in the lease deed. In the facts and circumstances of the case the trial Court as well as the appellate Court rightly did not find plaintiff's title in the suit land described in Schedule 2 of the plaint. 

 15. Admittedly, the CDA is the owner of Schedule 2 land, as such, in the absence of a definite proof of acquisition of title or interest by the plaintiff in Schedule 2 land and a corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the Schedule 2 land to the plaintiff, there cannot be any direction by the Court upon the CDA to grant lease of the excess land in favour of the plaintiff. In the frame of the suit the prayer for a direction upon the defendant CDA to grant lease of Schedule 2 land to the plaintiff appears to be barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The Courts below seriously erred in law in decreeing the suit on a casual view of the matter and without considering this vital legal question and the law bearing on the subject and the same has occasioned failure of justice. 

 17. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the opposite parties, has referred to me the case of S Zafar Ahmed vs. Abdul Khaliq,, reported in 16 DLR (WP, Karachi) 49. In this case their Lordships explained the scope of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Khondker next referred to me the case of Alamgir & others vs. Jainal Abedin, reported in 34 DLR 325. In this case also their Lordships explained the scope of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in giving relief to the aggrieved party under given circumstances. There is no dispute to the proposition of law enunciated by their Lordships that a Court exercising power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is competent to correct any error of law committed by any subordinate Court occasioning failure of justice. But the reported cited decisions appear to have no relevance to the facts of the present case and, as such, the cited decisions are of no assistance to the plaintiff-opposite party. 

 18. In this case the plaintiff filed the suit praying for getting lease of Schedule 2 land from the CDA. Subsequently, of course, the plaint was amended adding a prayer for declaration of title. Nowhere from the record it is found as to how the plaintiff acquired title in Schedule 2 land. It has been clearly admitted in paragraph No. 9 of the plaint that the plaintiff got settlement of 4.999 kathas of land on the basis of lease deed Ext. 2 and she acted on the same premises bona fide believing that the acquired title and interest in that quantum of land only and it never occurred to her that she got interest in 5.666 kathas of land till before the physical measurement of the suit land at the time of construction of her house thereon. It is thus evident that the additional 4.80 sqft of land was clearly beyond the contemplation and comprehension of the contending parties while concluding the lease deed Ext. 2. This excess land measuring 4.80 square feet thus clearly falls outside the purview of the lease agreement in question and consequently, the plaintiff cannot claim the same as a matter of right and the defendant CDA cannot be compelled to give settlement of the same to the plaintiff. It is thus crystal clear that the plaintiff did not acquire any title in Schedule 2 land. The only material question that remained for consideration by the Courts was whether the plaintiffs claim for getting lease of excess land contained in Schedule 2 of the plaint could be entertained and a direction from the Court to the CDA for granting such lease of the same in favour of the plaintiff could lawfully be made. Since I have already found that there is nothing on record to prove that the plaintiff has acquired any right and title in Schedule 2 land admittedly the CDA is the owner of Schedule 2 land, and there being no corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the same to the plaintiff, the Court cannot give a mandate compelling the defendant CDA to grant lease of the suit land to the plaintiff. Such a direction could be given only if a clear case was made out in favour of the plaintiff establishing a definite legal right for her for the enforcement of which the Court could come to her rescue in a properly constituted suit for Specific Performance of Contract. But, in the instant case, in the light of the case made out in the plaint and the evidence adduced at the trial I do not find any such legal right in favour of the plaintiff and a corresponding legal obligation on the part of the defendant CDA for granting lease of the Schedule 2 land to the plaintiff and, as such, the impugned decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge and subsequently affirmed by the learned appellate Court cannot be sustained in law. The impugned judgment is thus found to be neither legal nor proper and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the learned Courts below are not supported by the evidence on record and the law bearing on the subject and, as such, the same are not sustainable. For the reasons stated above the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the petitioners are sustained and those made by the learned Counsel for the opposite party are repelled. 

 19. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong in Title Appeal. No. 109 of 1989 affirming the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 96 of 1978 are set aside and Other Suit No. 96 of 1978 of the 2nd Court of the Assistant Judge, Chittagong is hereby dismissed.
